analysis.one_liner: Lets anyone buy a government-run Medicare health plan on the exchanges and lowers drug costs and out-of-pocket spending.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Rep. Jimmy Gomez with 7 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to three House committees and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create "Medicare Part E" — a government-run health plan that any U.S. resident could buy on the insurance exchanges and that employers could offer to workers, with gold-level benefits including abortion coverage regardless of state bans. It would also cap out-of-pocket costs for traditional Medicare at $6,700 a year, require the government to negotiate Medicare prescription drug prices (falling back to Veterans Affairs prices if talks fail), and enlarge ACA premium subsidies so households earning up to six times the poverty level qualify. A separate $30 billion fund would help states lower individual-market premiums and out-of-pocket costs.
analysis.who_benefits: People buying their own coverage would get a public plan option and larger subsidies, with eligibility stretched from 400% to 600% of the poverty line and credits recalculated against gold-level plans; workers whose employer plans are unaffordable would be referred to enrollment help; Medicare beneficiaries would gain a hard $6,700 cap on annual out-of-pocket costs; and Medicare Part D enrollees would benefit from government-negotiated drug prices. Low-income exchange customers would get deeper cost-sharing reductions, and individual-market premiums would be cushioned by the reinsurance fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Exchange enrollees, Medicare beneficiaries, and the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Creates a public "Medicare Part E" plan that any U.S. resident not already on Medicare, Medicaid, or CHIP could buy on the exchanges, and that employers could offer voluntarily, with the government keeping coverage portable if the worker loses the job.
Requires the plan to provide gold-level coverage and to cover abortions and all other reproductive services, overriding any state law that would prohibit that coverage.
Caps annual out-of-pocket cost-sharing for traditional Medicare (Parts A and B) at $6,700 starting in 2023, adjusted for medical inflation — traditional Medicare currently has no such cap.

Replaces the Medicare drug program's 'non-interference' clause with a mandate that HHS negotiate prices for high-cost Part D drugs, and if negotiation fails after a year, set the price at the lower of what the VA or Federal Supply Schedule pays.

Expands ACA premium tax credits to households earning up to 600% of poverty and rebases them to the second-lowest-cost gold plan, while deepening cost-sharing reductions for people between 100% and 400% of poverty.

Appropriates $30 billion for fiscal 2022-2024 for state reinsurance and affordability programs in the individual market, and applies premium rate-review and corrective-action authority to excessive or discriminatory rates, including in plans exempt from ACA rules.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund $2 billion in startup money, reserves, and the $30 billion reinsurance fund, plus the cost of much larger premium tax credits, with no offsetting revenue in the bill. Private health insurers would face a government-run competitor in the individual, small-group, and large-group markets plus stricter rate review. Brand-name drug makers would face Medicare price negotiation with a hard fallback to VA-level prices. Hospitals and doctors would be paid negotiated rates set between Medicare rates and exchange-market averages, and would lose balance-billing leverage in the public plan. Employers without affordable coverage would have to refer workers to enrollment navigators.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, private insurers, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates roughly $32 billion (a $2 billion startup fund plus a $30 billion reinsurance and affordability fund) and greatly enlarges premium tax credits without any offsetting revenue, so its cost would add directly to the deficit.

Part E premiums must fully finance the plan's benefits and administrative costs, and provider rates are set between Medicare rates and exchange-market averages — so the public plan's prices might not be much cheaper than private plans, and its savings are unproven.
The $30 billion reinsurance fund flows substantially to insurance companies as payments covering high-cost enrollees, subsidizing private insurers as well as lowering premiums.

The bill waives federal restrictions on using appropriated funds for reproductive health services, a provision that would itself draw opposition and litigation risk under some state laws, and it extends ACA-style rating rules into the large-employer market, where premiums for healthier groups could rise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefits are real and specific — a public option, a hard cap on Medicare out-of-pocket costs, negotiated drug prices, and much larger subsidies — but the bill pays for none of it, and the design routes significant public money through private insurers via the reinsurance fund while the public plan's pricing may yield only modest savings over private plans. It is a broad affordability package with an unfunded price tag, and as written it would probably have been rewritten heavily in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in three House committees and a health subcommittee from August 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023, never getting a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jimmy Gomez introduced the Choose Medicare Act on August 13, 2021, with six colleagues joining at introduction.
The same day, the House referred it to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor — and it was then referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
The action record shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind after that referral.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers kept the individual, small-group, and large-employer markets free of a government-run competitor, and drug makers kept Medicare barred from directly negotiating drug prices. Medicare beneficiaries and exchange customers gained nothing from the bill's death.

sides.party_line_note: Every supporter on record was a Democrat — the sponsor and 7 cosponsors, with no Republican sponsors — and because the bill never reached a vote, there are no roll calls to show where each party stood.

industries.note: A Medicare-run public plan would compete for customers in the individual, small-group, and large-employer markets, and insurers would face stronger rate review and potential rebates for excessive rates. The $30 billion reinsurance fund and richer subsidies would partly cushion them, but their core interest — no cheaper public alternative — runs against the bill.

HHS would have to negotiate prices for high-cost Part D drugs, with a fallback to VA or Federal Supply Schedule prices if negotiation fails — a direct cut to what manufacturers could charge. The same negotiated prices would apply to the public plan's drugs.

Every Medicare-participating provider would automatically be in the public plan's network, but would be paid negotiated rates between Medicare rates and exchange-market averages and would lose balance-billing rights in the plan. Guaranteed patient volume offsets some revenue loss.

Employers could voluntarily offer a Medicare-run plan to workers, and employers without affordable coverage would have to refer workers to enrollment navigators — a new option plus a small compliance duty.
